Existing consent frameworks assume a human who authorises an action in a context they can see. This paper asks what happens to a user's authorisation once their AI agent stops talking to humans and interacts primarily with other agents. Using the early-2026 Clawdbot/Moltbook incidents as a stress test, it argues that consent degrades as an operative governance mechanism once it travels through open-ended agent-to-agent chains, a condition the paper calls the *consent vacuum*: not the absence of consent, but the structural erosion of the conditions that make it meaningful.

The paper contributes a taxonomy of six consent-failure types; a distinction between visibility, auditability and intervenability as oversight capacities relevant to Article 14 of the EU AI Act; and a mapping onto the GDPR, the AI Act and the Digital Services Act, with the DSA systemic-risk regime offered as a structural template for governing emergent agent ecosystems.

IAIL 2026 was held in Brussels on 7 July 2026. Co-authored with Osman Gazi Güçlütürk (Galatasaray University, Faculty of Law).

Research area: [Agentic AI Safety & Governance](/research/agentic-ai-safety/).
